1 · Welcome

Heroes of Legend · Player’s Book

The door has held for a hundred years. Tonight, someone on the other side is knocking. Your companions look at you. You have a lantern, a scar that aches before rain, and one very bad idea that might get everyone through this alive.

Heroes of Legend is a fantasy roleplaying game about people who become remarkable through the choices they make. You might be a scholar who reads an opponent's stance like a page, a guardian who plants a shield in the only safe doorway, or a wanderer who calls the forest to your friends' defense. Your character is built from ancestry, experience, class and learned abilities. The combinations belong to you.

At the table

Each player speaks and acts for one hero. One participant is the Dungeon Architect, or DA: the person who describes the world, portrays the people and creatures in it, presents danger, and adjudicates uncertain situations. The DA tells you what your hero can perceive. You say what you try. Together, you discover what happens.

You do not need to act in a voice, memorize this book, or find a single correct solution. Ask questions. Describe a practical approach. Listen to what your companions want to attempt. A good plan can change the situation before anyone touches a die.

You will need three six-sided dice, and ideally three more for Boons and Banes. Consumable supplies use d4, d6, d8, d10, d12 and d20 inventory dice. Bring a character sheet, your learned abilities, something to record changes, and tokens or miniatures when a scene benefits from a square grid. A virtual tabletop can do the same work.

The promise of the game

Character development rewards planning. You choose which disciplines to study and which abilities make those studies useful. At the table, the chosen ability tells you what to do: its action, attribute, range, outcomes and limits are printed together. Your sword's appearance is yours to invent; the attack describes what it accomplishes.

Attacks connect. A poor roll changes how much harm and pressure an attack creates; it does not usually erase the turn. A stronger result may push an enemy away, expose a weakness, leave them burning, or put an ally where they need to be.

You recover HP after a safe breath, but wounds and spent Grit follow you. Victories can leave permanent scars. A hero who rises again is not untouched by what happened.

Learn one roll

When an uncertain action has consequences, roll 3d6 + one attribute. The six attributes are Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge and Reason. An ability names its attribute; otherwise the DA calls for the attribute that fits the attempt.

TotalResultWhat it means
8 or lessWeakMake the printed progress; you have not necessarily completed your purpose.
9–14StandardApply the Standard outcome.
15 or moreStrongApply the Strong outcome.

Three retained natural ones give Weak plus a complication. Three retained natural sixes give Strong plus a benefit. These exceptional results use the numbers on the dice, before adding your attribute.

Boons help and Banes hinder. Cancel one against one. Each remaining Boon adds a die; keep the highest three. Each remaining Bane adds a die; keep the lowest three. Use at most three net extra dice. Add your attribute after choosing the three dice. Difficulty changes the dice you keep, not the Weak/Standard/Strong boundaries.

> Example — a dangerous crossing. Lira has Agility +2. The DA asks for Agility > to cross a crumbling beam before the pursuers arrive. The rotten surface adds > 1 Bane; an ally's secured rope supplies 1 Boon. They cancel. Lira rolls 2, 4, 5: > 11 + 2 = 13, a Standard result. She reaches the far ledge as agreed before the roll. > If there were no danger or meaningful cost, the group could simply describe crossing.

A moment of play

DA: The broken bridge ends two squares short of the far bank. Water roars below. The rider behind you is reaching for a horn.

Lira: I have room to run. Can I jump the gap?

DA: Your Agility is +2, so your running broad jump reaches four squares. There is a clear landing. Spend the movement and you are across; no roll needed.

Borin: I cannot leave Oren behind. I plant myself between him and the rider. I use Defend and keep my Reaction ready.

Oren: I use Force on the jammed bridge mechanism. Can we lower the remaining span?

DA: Yes. It needs two progress. A Weak result loosens it, but the rider will have time to sound the horn. A Standard or Strong result opens it now.

Oren: Brawn +0. I roll 3, 4, 5: twelve. Standard, two progress.

DA: The catch tears loose. The span drops with a crack, giving you a route across. The rider lowers the horn and draws a blade instead.

This is play: make choices in the fiction, apply the rule that fits, and let the result change what can happen next. Force is an action Oren chooses. Brawn is the attribute the action tells him to roll.

Find your way through the book

Read Create Your Hero to build from the beginning, or choose one of the six ready-to-play heroes near the back. Ancestries, origins and classes supply your first choices. Disciplines show how to qualify for learned abilities. Playing the Game explains combat; Beyond the Battlefield covers the rest of an adventurer's life.

Keep your own abilities close at hand. You do not need to memorize everyone else's catalog. The universal actions are available to every character, provided they have any required equipment. A learned card does not replace the ordinary permission to try something anyone could reasonably attempt.

Before the first adventure

Agree on the tone of the campaign and why your heroes travel together. Discuss what kinds of danger, injury and horror people want included or left offstage. Anyone can ask to pause a scene or change an uncomfortable detail. The wound tables describe fictional injuries; their descriptions can be adjusted while retaining the rules.

Choose names, something each hero wants, and a connection between companions. Decide how to share maps and record supplies. The DA should explain what your characters already know about the first destination. You can discover the rest in play.

> About this edition. This is the complete player-facing level 1–10 playtest > manuscript. The current catalog is approved for playtesting. It is intended > for real table feedback; numerical balance remains open to refinement. Record > unclear situations for feedback to the designer. The companion Dungeon > Architect’s Guide & Bestiary is included in the starter kit.

2 · Create Your Hero

Heroes of Legend · Player’s Book

Begin with a person you want to play: an armored healer, an eloquent duelist, a hunter who speaks with ghosts. Decide what they want, then choose how they pursue it.

Character creation has two stages. Level 0 is your life before choosing a class. Level 1 is the completed adventurer you bring to the first session. Finish and close the level-0 ledger before making level-1 purchases. Both stages have their own DP pool; unused points expire separately.

Before making purchases, turn to @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.b84fcd9536c51a01]{Disciplines and Character Paths}. It explains what discipline ranks mean and how they qualify you for abilities. Keep that chapter and your intended class entry handy as you build.

1. Assign attributes

Assign a value from −2 to +2 to each of the six attributes. Their total must be +3. A straightforward starting array is +2, +1, +1, +0, +0, −1, arranged as you choose. Check your intended class's minimums before settling the array.

AttributeCommon uses
BrawnExert strength, use Force, climb and make many melee attacks.
FortitudeEndure harm, resist bodily threats and make death rolls; contributes to HP.
AgilityMove deftly, remain Hidden, jump and make many ranged attacks; contributes to Speed.
GuileDeceive, misdirect, improvise and exploit an opening.
KnowledgeApply learning, recognize patterns, craft and use learned techniques.
ReasonNotice details, perceive danger, judge a situation and keep your thinking clear.

These are not exclusive lists. Roll the attribute printed on the ability you use. Some techniques deliberately use an unusual attribute, such as Knowledge for a carefully studied attack. There is no added skill rating.

Your chosen attributes stay fixed as you gain levels. Explicit items can modify an attribute while their rules apply. Ordinary published item adjustments run no higher than +2 or lower than −2, but can move your total outside the creation range. Matching bonuses do not add together: use the largest. A curse can explicitly suppress bonuses or set a value instead. Item changes never revise your creation DP.

2. Choose ancestry

Choose Human, Elf, Dwarf or Halfling. Record the ancestry's HP contribution and base Speed, then choose two of its five traits. Read the exact benefits: a description of keen eyes does not grant an extra sense unless the rules say so.

AncestryHP contributionBase SpeedStarting coin contribution
Human+26+1
Elf+26+2
Dwarf+45+2
Halfling+15+0

Any ancestry can grow up in any culture. Your ancestry is not a compulsory profession, personality or allegiance.

3. Choose culture and background

Your culture describes the community that shaped you. Your background describes part of your life or work before adventuring. Choose one of each from the origin chapter, then select one complete paired option from each. A pair grants a rank-1 discipline and its accompanying ability. Do not take the rank from one pair and the ability from another.

A granted ability supplies its stated prerequisite grants. Record the ranks before buying anything. If a grant duplicates something you already have, receive 1 DP for that stage. It does not raise the rank, give an unrestricted replacement, or carry forward after the stage ends.

Record Common and one ordinary language learned in your home community, then apply explicit extra language grants. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.0237eee3512bbfa9]{Languages} for the shared list, spoken-only grants and campaign alternatives.

4. Spend level-0 DP

Your level-0 pool is 10 + Knowledge + Reason + Guile, plus any duplicate-grant compensation. Negative attributes reduce this pool too. Buy eligible Novice abilities at their printed price: normally 2 DP, or 1 DP for the six shared exceptions in @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.efd0799a6387e823]{Abilities}. Their printed requirements must already be met by your origin grants. You may not buy discipline ranks at level 0.

Record each purchase in order. Buy any eligible kind of ability. One or two attacks can define your fighting style, leaving room for talents useful between battles. If you have an odd point left, a 1-DP ability can put it to use; these choices remain available at later levels too.

Close the stage. Unused level-0 DP expires. Your future class cannot qualify a purchase you made earlier.

5. Choose a class

Choose one class. Both of its required attributes must be at least 0; Odd has no minimums. Record its HP contribution and discipline prices. Choose two distinct rank-1 disciplines from its starting list, applying duplicate compensation where appropriate. Choose one of its three level-1 signature abilities.

Your class sets discipline prices and signature access. You can buy any eligible shared ability. There is no multiclassing.

6. Spend level-1 DP

Start a new pool of 10 + Knowledge + Reason + Guile, plus level-1 duplicate compensation. Now you can purchase discipline ranks at your class's prices as well as eligible abilities. You must buy ranks sequentially: rank 2 requires owning rank 1, and rank 3 requires owning rank 2. There is no additional level gate on ranks.

Your class entry lists the price of every discipline rank. The comparison table in @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.b84fcd9536c51a01]{Disciplines and Character Paths} shows all classes together. Each price buys that rank alone. For example, a Blade pays 1 DP for Arms 1 and 2 DP for Arms 2, spending 3 DP to learn both from scratch. A rank grants no action or bonus by itself; it qualifies you to learn abilities.

All card prerequisites must be owned before purchase, not merely before use. You can own an item whose requirements you do not meet, but cannot use the gated capability. A flaming sword's special power does not become available simply because you found it.

Close the stage. Unused level-1 DP expires. Later levels allow saving DP.

> Example — two separate budgets. A hero with Knowledge +1, Reason +1 and Guile −1 > gets 11 DP at each creation stage. At level 0, five Novice purchases cost 10 and > the last point expires. At level 1, a duplicate class rank adds 1 to the new pool, > making 12. Buying a discipline rank priced at 3 DP and four Novice cards for 8 spends 11; > the remaining point also expires. Nothing from the first stage was borrowed.

7. Resolve equipment and recipes

Read every acquisition line. Some learned cards grant an ordinary item when first acquired. A grant supplies the compatible basic item only if you do not already own it. Three attacks that require a melee weapon can share the same weapon; they do not generate three free weapons. The same principle applies when you learn training later. Selling an item does not reactivate its old grant.

Describe your weapon now. A sword, axe or stout staff can express the same permitted melee attacks. Its ordinary appearance changes no damage. A ranged attack still requires compatible ranged equipment. Most ordinary melee and ranged weapons use 1 Bulk each. Special items add only their printed effects.

Choose any recipes explicitly granted by crafting cards. Recipe knowledge is not a free finished product or a supply of ingredients. Record tools, materials and future recipe opportunities separately.

8. Finish your numbers

RecordCalculation
Maximum HP12 + ancestry HP + class HP + Fortitude + explicit benefits
Capacity10 + 3 × Brawn
EncumbranceCarried Bulk above capacity, minimum 0
SpeedAncestry base + Agility − encumbrance, minimum 0
Stability0 unless an explicit grant raises it; highest source, cap 3
Starting Grit2, plus any explicitly purchased increase
Starting wounds / death marks0 / 0

HP does not automatically grow each level. A purchase such as Conditioned Body can increase it within that card's limits. Record current and maximum HP separately. Record your highest resistance for each damage type, never a sum of matching armor.

> Example — Borin's pack. Borin is a dwarf Protector with Fortitude +2. His base > maximum HP is 12 + 4 + 5 + 2 = 23. His chosen trait and Conditioned Body each add > 1, giving 25. Brawn +1 gives capacity 13. His 11 Bulk fits, so Agility +0 leaves > his dwarf base Speed at 5. Armor does not automatically add Stability.

9. Take coins and shop

Starting coins are 40 + ancestry + culture + background + class contributions. The Starting Coins reference at the end of this chapter gives the exact additions. This produces 50–70 coins before shopping. Resolve equipment grants first. Everyone begins with a plain worn outfit; a pack, supplies and potion are purchases unless explicitly granted.

Use the market. Record coins spent, coins left, supply dice and every item's Bulk. A container does not cancel its contents' Bulk. Decide which items are held. A bow, a two-handed weapon, or weapon and shield can leave no free hand for healing. Sharing a rope or light is practical; somebody still carries it.

10. Put a person on the sheet

Name your hero and give them a reason to stay with the party. Put your most-used actions on your first reference page. All learned cards remain available; there is no prepared-card hand limit.

Before play, check both DP ledgers, requirements, grants, Bulk, free hands and class minimums. The six complete characters near the back show every step.

Growing into a legend

The DA awards levels at milestones. At level 2 and every later level, receive 8 + your new level DP. Save these points or spend them in a place the DA agrees is safe. Mental attributes modify only the two creation pools, not these awards.

New levelDP awardOther universal milestone
210—
311+1 Grit; choose a level-3 class signature; Adept cards available
412—
513—
614—
715+1 Grit; choose a level-7 class signature; Master cards available
816—
917—
1018—

Novice, Adept and Master abilities normally cost 2, 4 and 8 DP and require minimum levels 1, 3 and 7. Novice purchases are explicitly permitted during level-0 creation. The six shared 1-DP abilities keep their printed price at every level. Higher tiers do not require an earlier card in a chain. Mixed requirements mean you need every listed rank. Class signatures require only their class and level; extra eligible signatures can be purchased for the same tier price.

Your Grit increases are universal experience, not class features. They do not refund previous expenditure. A once-only learned card can grant one additional Grit. Ordinary rest does not refresh Grit. Your abilities, scars and choices tell the story of the hero you become.

Use the current catalog choices and the advancement rules below.

1. Assign six attributes from −2 to +2, totaling +3. These stay fixed; magic items may modify them but do not retroactively change creation benefits. 2. Choose ancestry and two of its five traits. Choose culture independently. 3. At level 0 choose one culture pair and one background pair. Each grants a discipline at rank 1 and its paired ability, including its requirements. 4. Receive 10 + Knowledge + Reason + Guile DP, including negative adjustments. Buy eligible Novice cards; no discipline purchases. Spend or lose this pool. 5. At level 1 choose a class, meeting minimum 0 in both required attributes; Odd has no minimums. Choose two distinct listed rank-1 disciplines and a class-exclusive level-1 signature. 6. Receive a fresh 10 + Knowledge + Reason + Guile DP. Duplicate grants give 1 DP each for that stage, not a replacement choice or automatic higher rank. Buy ranks at class prices and eligible abilities. Spend or lose the pool. 7. Resolve explicit equipment and recipe grants. One compatible weapon can serve several attacks; do not grant or count it twice. Describe its appearance now. 8. HP = 12 + ancestry contribution + class contribution + Fortitude + explicit chosen benefits. Capacity = 10 + 3 × Brawn. Every Bulk above capacity reduces Speed by 1. Speed = ancestry base + Agility − that penalty, minimum 0.

Record Stability 0 unless an explicit chosen trait, ability or item grants more. Use the highest applicable value, maximum 3; do not derive it from attributes.

Grit begins at 2 at level 1, plus one at levels 3 and 7. Grit expenditure persists; a purchased once-only card may grant another point. There is no class-based automatic attribute or HP growth. Small HP purchases are explicitly limited per level.

DA awards milestone levels. Level 2 onward grants 8 + new level DP; bank it, spend only in a DA-approved safe place. Tier 1/3/7 cards normally cost 2/4/8 DP. The six @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.c0c043f22d65aa20]{1-DP shared abilities} are Novice exceptions: no discipline requirements, purchase once each, available at level 0 and later. Ranks must be purchased sequentially; no additional rank level gates. Cards have no prerequisite card chains. Receive one chosen class signature at 3 and 7; only class and level qualify it. No multiclassing or access to another class’s signatures.

Coins are one currency. The agreed target is 50–70 starting coins after card grants. The @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.880380bcd80cfec6]{starting allocation} is 40 + ancestry + culture + background + class. After resolving grants, use the @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.cfa94361944ba875]{market}, record purchases, remaining coins, carried Bulk and occupied hands. The plain worn outfit is a universal starting baseline; packs and potions are purchased, not free. Gear sells for half price or trades at full value with a willing trader.

Language reference

The @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.0237eee3512bbfa9]{language defaults} supply Common plus one ordinary home language, followed by explicit extra grants. Apply explicit ancestry grants separately; culture choices do not restrict language.

Ledger to copy

Keep the sequence: a class grant cannot qualify a level-0 purchase retroactively.

Agreed target: 50–70 coins after card-granted equipment. Proposed allocation: the values below.

Starting coins = 40 + ancestry + culture + background + class.

Add these once after completing level 1. This is a starting purse, not income each level. It does not use DP or attributes. Resolve card equipment grants before shopping; there is no coin reimbursement for a duplicate or declined grant.

Contributions represent what the character brings on departure: savings, community support, prior work and preparation. They are not innate ancestry wealth, a moral ranking of cultures or a continuing class stipend. The largest ancestry difference is two coins. These allocations describe preparation, not biology.

You step your guard into the line of the strike and wave your companion behind you as it lands.

Rules

Action: Reaction · Attribute: None — no roll

Target / range / shape: One adjacent willing ally, after a single-target attack is declared against it but before rolling.

Become the target if you meet the attack’s range and targeting requirements. Resolve the attack once against you; your ally receives none of its effects. Afterward the ally may move up to 2 squares without provoking if able. You do not move to intercept and cannot redirect an area attack.

Duration: The triggering attack and immediate ally movement.

Equipment / acquisition: None.

5 · Disciplines and Character Paths

Heroes of Legend · Player’s Book

A discipline is a field of study. An ability is something you have learned to do with it. Your hero might study Arms to practice martial techniques, Life to restore others, or Scholarship to understand and exploit what others overlook.

Ranks run from 1 to 3 and must be bought in order. There is no level gate on a rank, but the ability you want may require level 3 or 7. Read the requirements before spending: Arms 2 and Subterfuge 1 means you must own both. A rank by itself grants no action, equipment, attribute bonus or unrestricted use of that discipline's cards.

Your class makes some disciplines easier to develop than others. A Blade learns martial techniques readily; an Arcanist has a shorter road into elemental magic. Both can study beyond those strengths. Abilities themselves cost the same DP at each tier, whatever your class.

Buying ranks

You cannot buy disciplines at level 0. After choosing your class, use the table on the following reference page or the prices in your class entry. Each cell lists the separate costs of rank 1 / rank 2 / rank 3, in DP. Buy them in order.

A Blade learning Arms from scratch pays 1 DP for rank 1, then 2 DP for rank 2, then 4 DP for rank 3: 7 DP altogether. That same Blade pays 3, 6 and 12 DP for Life. Odd pays 2 / 4 / 8 DP for every discipline.

The discipline cards below describe each field. These shared purchase rules apply to all eighteen disciplines. Each symbol also appears on ability headers; the small number over its lower edge is the required rank.

Choose a direction

Imagine what you want to do for the company. A healer might protect a retreat, restore HP, treat lasting injuries, or combine all three. A nature-focused hero might become a beast, command an animal, control the ground, or guide companions through dangerous country. These are different choices even when they share a theme.

The four character paths that follow show different ways to build a hero: a Thinking Fighter, Green Healer, Spellblade and Light-Fingered Adventurer. They are examples, not subclasses. Mix them freely where you meet the requirements. The listed cards do not waive DP, tier or discipline requirements, and a suggested future card is not part of your starting equipment.

Keep a few abilities ready for the scenes you expect most often. You may know several attacks, but you still have only the actions you can spend. A useful Maneuver, Reaction, travel skill or social technique can matter more than another similar Main Action.

6 · Playing the Game

Heroes of Legend · Player’s Book

A drawn blade changes the conversation. A broken bridge changes the journey. The rules help you decide what those changes mean when timing, danger and the choices of several characters meet.

Begin with what your hero is doing. You can use a learned ability, take a universal action, or describe something the situation makes possible. The DA establishes the circumstances and calls for a roll only when uncertainty has consequences.

Resolve an action

When you use an ability, declare it before rolling. Read its requirements, choose its targets and any printed options, and check range and equipment. Spend the action and any required cost. Roll its attribute if instructed, then apply the complete Weak, Standard or Strong outcome. Finally, record conditions and continuing effects.

An outcome is complete: do not add the Weak damage to the Standard damage. If a Strong outcome includes an earlier benefit, it says so. Instant damage happens once; a condition applied by that damage follows the condition's own timing.

A no-roll ability still costs its printed action. A treatment that takes an hour cannot be completed in one combat turn merely because it is indexed as a Main Action.

Boons, Banes and results

Roll three dice, plus one die for each net Boon or Bane, to a maximum of six dice. With Boons, retain the best three; with Banes, retain the worst three. Add the printed attribute once. Weak is 8 or less, Standard 9–14, and Strong 15 or more.

CircumstanceUsual adjustment
Meaningful help or obstacle1 Boon or Bane
Substantial help or a severe obstacle2 Boons or Banes
Exceptional advantage or difficulty, still possible3 Boons or Banes

These are guides for the DA. They do not turn an impossible attempt into a possible one. Do not count the same obstacle twice under different names. Boons and Banes from distinct valid sources stack, cancel, and then use the three-die net limit.

> Example — keeping the best three. An attack has 3 Boons and 1 Bane, leaving > 2 Boons. Roll five dice. On 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, retain 4, 5, 6 for 15. Brawn +1 makes > 16, a Strong result. If two Banes remained instead, retain 1, 2, 4 for 7; Brawn +1 > would give 8, a Weak result. Neither roll changes the attack's printed damage.

Read retained natural 111 as Weak with an additional complication and 666 as Strong with an additional benefit. The result still makes its printed progress. The DA fits a benefit or complication to the scene; it does not silently double damage or grant another action.

Taking turns

At the start of combat, one player rolls unmodified 3d6. On 12 or more, the player side acts first. Otherwise the opposing side begins. This determines which side starts every round of this combat; do not roll again each round.

The starting side chooses one of its characters to act. Then the other side chooses one. Alternate until everyone has taken a turn. If one side has no characters left to act, the other finishes its remaining turns. A character takes one turn each round. Each side chooses its order as it goes.

On your turn, you have one Main Action, one Maneuver, and movement up to your Speed. You also have one Reaction, available for its stated trigger. Refresh that turn's budget at the start of your turn. A defense roll does not itself spend a Reaction. Choose your retained categories at turn start if Dazed or Grappled.

You can split movement around your actions. You can convert your Main Action into a Maneuver and a Maneuver into another movement allowance. Conversion goes only in that direction. Converting your Main and original Maneuver into movement gives three total movement allowances: a full sprint.

> Example — reaching an ally. Speed 6 lets Mara move 6 squares. She converts her > Maneuver into movement for 6 more, then uses her Main Action to heal a companion. > She has not gained a second Main Action, and any difficult terrain costs still apply.

A Reaction resolves when its trigger says it does, including on someone else's turn. Once spent, it is unavailable until refreshed. A free attack granted by an ability spends no action and may occur more than once in a turn, but free attacks never trigger additional free attacks. Read the granting effect to see which attack it allows.

Attacking and defending

Players roll. When your hero attacks, roll the attack's printed attribute and read its attacker outcomes. This is true even if the target is another player character; the receiving player does not also roll a defense.

When a DA-controlled creature attacks you, roll the defense attribute specified by that attack. It might be Agility to evade a blow, Fortitude to withstand a bodily assault, or another attribute named by the attack. Apply the result from its Weak defense / Standard defense / Strong defense columns. Weak defense is the most dangerous outcome; Strong defense is the least dangerous.

Player's defenseEquivalent attacker outcome
WeakStrong attack
StandardStandard attack
StrongWeak attack

Creature Evasion adds its printed Boons or Banes to your attack. Threat adds its printed Boons or Banes to your defense against that creature's attack. These use the ordinary dice rules; do not add them numerically to the total.

If you control a summon, roll that creature's printed attributes. Its player profile already presents attack outcomes in the correct direction. Your hero's own Brawn or Reason does not replace the summon’s value.

For NPC-only actions, a player or the DA assuming the player role rolls. For an NPC attack against another NPC, roll the defender’s printed attribute and read the attacker’s defense-outcome table. For consequential healing or another task, roll the acting NPC’s attribute. Make one roll; handling dice does not transfer control of the NPC. Off-screen events can use DA judgment.

Damage and resistance

Damage comes from the chosen outcome, not a weapon damage die. Your attribute has already affected the roll; do not add it again to damage. Apply each matching resistance after determining the outcome. Armor DR is physical resistance.

Use the highest applicable resistance of each type, to a maximum of 3. Two sources of physical resistance 2 do not give 4. Physical resistance 2 and Fire resistance 1 can apply together because they protect against different types.

A damaging event always deals at least 1 total damage after resistance. This minimum applies to the event, not separately to every component. It does not create damage for a harmless ability. Conditions, pushes and other riders still apply unless their own rules prevent them.

> Example — steel and flame. An attack deals 3 physical and 1 fire damage. > Physical resistance 2 reduces the physical portion to 1. Fire resistance 1 removes > the fire portion. Take 1 total damage, not one of each type. If both portions had > been reduced to zero, the event would still deal its minimum 1 total damage.

Physical includes impacts, sonic force and supernatural force when the attack says physical. Fire, Cold and Lightning have separate resistances even though their wounds share the Elemental table. Life resistance also reduces ordinary HP healing.

Same-kind numerical bonuses do not add together unless explicitly stated. Conditions with meaningful ratings can add; binary Prone cannot. Boons and Banes use their own stacking rules. Weakness X adds X to its matching damage component before resistance, once per event. Use the highest value of each type, normally capped at 3. It cannot add a damage type absent from the attack. Special vulnerabilities use their printed procedure. Fire Weakness 2 turns 3 fire damage into 5 before resistance; it adds nothing to a purely physical attack.

Shields and guarded positions

Defend is a universal Maneuver that gives 1 Boon to defenses until the start of your next turn. Repeating Defend does not increase that same benefit.

Shield Block spends a Reaction before an eligible defense. While you use the held shield, gain 1 Boon to defenses against attacks the DA judges it can block, until the start of your next turn. Most ordinary physical attacks can be blocked. Defend and Shield Block are separate sources: together they supply 2 Boons. Creatures use shields the same way.

Opportunity attacks

Leaving an enemy's melee reach voluntarily, casting beside it, standing, stowing an item, or retrieving an item can provoke. The enemy may spend its Reaction to make Basic Melee, never a specialty card. Resolve that attack at the start of the provoking action, before the original action takes effect.

Then continue the original action if its actor is capable. Damage alone does not cancel it. An actor reduced to Dying cannot continue. Commit the action on declaration; if interrupted permanently, that action is spent. Additional HP or item costs are paid only when the action continues into resolution. An unspent potion is not drunk by an interrupted character who can no longer act.

Drawing a weapon as part of attacking adds no separate action. Dropping an item is free. Stowing or picking up an item costs a Maneuver. Forced movement never provokes. An ability can explicitly allow movement without provoking.

> Example — a spell under pressure. Vaelis begins casting beside an armed foe. > The foe spends its Reaction on Basic Melee. Vaelis makes the required defense and > loses HP. Still conscious and otherwise capable, Vaelis continues the spell and > pays any remaining printed cost. A healing spell cannot proceed if its upfront > life cost would leave its caster at 0 HP.

Distance, space and cover

All distances use squares. A square is the useful unit for your map; it does not require a fixed conversion into feet or meters. A diagonal step costs one square. Normal ground costs 1 movement; difficult ground costs 2.

You cannot move through an occupied square unless its occupant is Prone. That square costs 2 movement, and you cannot end there. Standing costs 2 movement. An ability that moves you without provoking still respects terrain, occupied spaces and legal endpoints unless it explicitly says otherwise.

A target you must see must actually be visible. An attack also needs a path to it. Partial obstruction gives 1 Bane; heavy cover gives 3 Banes. Heavy cover still leaves a narrow attack path, such as fighting from behind a wall or dense thicket. A solid barrier with no attack path prevents that attack. Concealment that prevents you from seeing a sight-required target is not merely heavy cover.

For a player area attack, choose the printed range, shape, inclusion and exclusions. Roll once using the worst applicable net Boon/Bane situation among its targets. Use that result for all targets; apply their resistances individually. When an NPC area attack affects several players, each player makes their own defense roll.

Push, pull and throw

A push moves a target away; a pull brings it toward the source. Follow a card's specific direction and shape. Apply Stability once to the initial target, reducing the available forced movement, to a minimum of 0. Stability is normally 0; only an explicit grant increases it. Use the highest source, maximum 3.

Spend the entered square's terrain cost from the movement budget. If any positive budget remains, the target enters the final square even if its cost exceeds that budget, then stops. For example, push 1 can enter one difficult square and stop. Stability does not reduce Prone, conditions, voluntary movement, projectile range, obstacle progress or the reduction of a grapple.

A collision with another movable creature forms a moving group. Apply collision damage to the participants using movement remaining on contact, then subtract the new creature's Stability once before continuing. The group moves together; do not charge the same creature's Stability twice in that movement. A hard obstruction stops the group and deals remaining-budget collision damage +1 to each member. The original mover then bounces one square in the opposite direction if possible.

> Example — Stability in a chain. Push 5 strikes Stability 1, leaving 4. After > one normal square, 3 remains. The moving creature strikes a new creature with > Stability 2. Resolve the contact, subtract 2, and use the remaining 1 to move the > group one further normal square. If the attack also inflicted Burning, stopping > the movement would not remove that condition.

> Crowded collisions. Moving groups must finish in separate legal spaces. > If everyone cannot fit, stop at the last position where they can; the DA decides > the arrangement. Placement cannot pass through walls or grant extra forward > movement. The original mover’s backward bounce still applies where possible.

Grappling and capture

Grappling requires a learned ability; it is not automatically granted with Basic Melee. Grappled prevents movement. At ratings 1, 2 and 3, retain respectively two, one or none of Main Action, Maneuver and Reaction, chosen at turn start. The grappler is restricted by their own contribution as well. Multiple grapplers' contributions add on the target. Attacks against a Grappled target gain Boons equal to its rating.

If you still have a Main Action, Force can reduce your grapple by 1/2/3. Grappled 3 needs outside help. A grappler can freely release their own contribution. A grapple is maintained and does not simply decay at turn end.

Attacks are lethal by default. Taking a prisoner requires a printed nonlethal ability, grappling or restraint. Once a helpless captive is secured and no combat remains, return to ordinary narration. You do not need to keep taking turns to conduct a conversation.

Ending a fight

A fight ends when the immediate opposition is resolved, not because everyone decides to ignore an active death roll. Resolve Dying before leaving combat timing. When it is safe to pause and companions can attend to an ordinary fire or similar immediate hazard, settle that hazard as the scene allows. Other conditions remain until their own removal, expiry or remedy. A safe breath restores HP; it does not remove wounds, refund Grit, cure every condition or reverse Last Words.

These summarize the approved system. Bruce resolves discrepancies; current cards and rules are the source, not earlier editions.

Resolution

Roll only for uncertainty with consequences. Correct fictional action may reveal a clue without a roll. The DA asks for Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge or Reason; the player takes an action which may call for that roll. Force is an action, not another attribute or a separate skill-roll category.

Roll 3d6 plus one attribute. Weak is 8 or below: progress, not automatic success. Standard is 9–14. Strong is 15 or above. Three natural retained sixes give Strong plus a benefit; three retained ones give Weak plus a complication.

Boons and Banes cancel. Use at most three net extra dice, retaining the best or worst three. Difficulty comes through Banes, never another target number on the same roll. A cumulative task’s progress target is a different thing: 1/2/3 progress per Weak/Standard/Strong result.

Turns and attacks

At combat start, one unmodified 3d6: 12+ gives players the first turn, otherwise the opposing side starts. Alternate sides; each side chooses its next character. The same side starts every round. Each character has Main, Maneuver, Reaction and movement. Main converts to Maneuver, Maneuver to movement; never upward.

Player attacks use one attacker roll, even against a player. NPC attacks use the player’s defense roll. Strong defense receives Weak attack effects, Standard receives Standard, Weak receives Strong. The defense itself spends no Reaction. Players roll their controlled creatures’ printed attack and defense attributes. For NPC-only actions, either a player or the DA assuming the player role rolls. For an NPC-versus-NPC attack, roll the defender’s printed defense attribute and read the attacker’s defense-outcome table. For consequential NPC healing or other tasks, roll the acting NPC’s printed attribute and outcomes. Apply the ordinary modifiers and use one roll; handling the dice does not transfer control of the NPC. Off-screen events may be resolved by DA judgment without simulating combat.

Damage is fixed by the card. Apply the highest resistance of each matching type, cap 3; do not sum matching armor. Minimum 1 damage applies to the whole damaging event, not each component. Physical is one type. Different resistances coexist. Conditions and displacement may matter more than a larger damage number.

Numerical weakness — approved October 16, 2026: Weakness X increases the matching damage component by X before resistance. Apply each weakness once per damaging event. Use the highest applicable weakness of each type, not the sum of multiple sources, with a normal cap of 3. A damaging effect must include that type; weakness does not add an absent damage type.

Example: Fire Weakness 2 changes 3 fire damage to 5 before resistance. An event dealing 4 physical and 1 fire instead becomes 4 physical and 3 fire; an event dealing only 4 physical is unchanged. Apply matching resistances next.

Special vulnerabilities, such as fire stopping regeneration, use their printed procedure. They do not imply numerical weakness or extra damage unless stated.

Movement

Normal squares cost 1, difficult 2. Diagonal movement costs 1. Standing costs 2 movement. Cannot cross an occupied square unless its occupant is prone; then cost 2 and never end there. Forced movement consumes the entered terrain’s cost; any positive remaining budget can enter the final square and stop even if that cost exceeds the budget.

Forced collisions gather movable occupants into one moving group. All take the collision damage using movement remaining at contact, before deducting the newly struck creature’s Stability. If movement remains, the group continues together. A hard obstruction stops the group and adds 1 to remaining-budget collision damage. The original mover bounces one square opposite afterward if possible.

Group placement — approved October 16, 2026: move the group along the forced movement path and finish in separate legal spaces. If everyone cannot fit, stop at the last position where they can. The DA determines the exact arrangement; placement cannot pass through walls or grant extra forward movement. The original mover’s backward bounce still applies where possible.

All actors have @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.3292b6a49dcf7236]{Stability}: default 0, explicit grants only, maximum 3, highest source. It consumes forced movement once per newly struck creature, including through a collision chain; no protection against Prone or conditions.

Conditions

Resolve a temporary numbered condition at turn end, then reduce by 1. Burning and Freezing deal their rating in matching elemental damage; Bleeding bypasses resistance. Poisoned applies its rating in Banes, not damage. Frightened supplies Banes while the stated source is perceptible. Slowed reduces Speed.

Dazed 1/2/3 leaves two/one/no categories among Main, Maneuver and Reaction; choose at turn start. Movement remains. Paralyzed stops actions and movement at any positive rating; its number is duration. Blinded and Deafened numbers are duration, not severity. An asterisk prevents automatic decay; a persistent binary sense loss needs only rating 1*. Removal follows the source.

Grappled prevents movement and reduces action choices like Dazed; it is maintained, not decaying. The grappler suffers their own contribution too. Force can reduce Grappled while Main is retained; rating 3 needs help. Attacks gain Boons equal to the actual target’s Grappled rating. Greater restriction applies when combined with Dazed, not their sum. Prone is binary. Hidden is universal, not observer-by-observer.

A mixed permanent/temporary bookkeeping rule is recorded in the full condition reference. Do not let a new temporary effect become permanent merely because another is starred.

Summons, exploration and recovery

Summoned forms — approved October 16, 2026: summons are shaped from energies to resemble and act like their creatures, not actual physical creatures brought into the scene. They cannot be healed and disappear at 0 HP, leaving no body. Ordinary unsummoned creatures retain their own healing rules.

Summoned forms remain tangible: they occupy squares, block movement, take damage and can be pushed or grappled normally unless their card says otherwise. Their energy composition grants no automatic incorporeality or damage/control immunity.

Summons require commands; see the @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.9ff12960a5e160cc]{summoning reference}. Without a command they do nothing, including following, lookout and alerts. Old orders grant no continued activity; existing conditions and durations still resolve. No free independent turns, inherent Reactions or summon chains. No count cap. Beyond 6 squares from the controller they disappear, including forced movement of either participant. Measure between the nearest occupied squares of controller and summon, using ordinary grid distance; this applies to every footprint. Exactly 6 squares is within the tether; beyond 6 causes immediate disappearance.

Summoned healing — approved October 16, 2026: the controller pays the healing ability’s printed HP cost instead of the summon, once, before resolution. Payment bypasses resistance and must leave the controller above 0 HP. Use the summon’s printed attribute and outcomes. Ordinary unsummoned healers pay their own cost.

Ordinary travel has no routine roll and no exhaustion track. Group checks occur outside combat only: each participant adds 1/2/3 to a declared target. State binary or cumulative before rolling. No group crafting, recipe derivation or wound treatment.

After a safe breath, restore full HP. Grit expenditure and wounds persist. Player characters enter Dying at 0; creatures normally die there. Attacks are lethal unless an explicit ability permits a different outcome; grapple/restraint can capture.

@UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.9303127ab1b28c3b]{Recovery boundary} records what is preserved and what still needs a complete standalone reference before this draft is used without the agreed spec.

@UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.f5003d6e49eeed0c]{Latest perception, timing and movement decisions} supersede earlier timing notes. @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.b8dbac21301a8aa3]{Full conditions}, @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.401d23f4b66980ee]{wounds}, and @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.7039600a66195489]{encounter calibration} complete the current working references.

Player rolls — agreed

When a player looks for something, the DA calls for Reason, with Boons/Banes for circumstances. When someone might perceive a hidden player character, that player rolls Agility to remain Hidden. Do not add an opposed observer roll. Ordinary obvious information requires no roll. Hidden remains universal; actual concealment and a plausible approach matter.

Procedure: active searching or attempting to hide during combat costs a Main Action unless a card states otherwise. A hidden creature that attacks or openly reveals itself loses Hidden. No roll conceals someone in plain view with no plausible concealment. Establish progress and consequences before an unscripted roll. A Weak search might narrow the location; a Weak hiding attempt might reach cover while leaving evidence. These examples do not override the scene or a card’s printed outcomes.

Opportunities — agreed

Starting a provoking action triggers the opportunity attack before that action resolves. Resolve Basic Melee using the attacker’s normal player-roll procedure; no specialty attack. Then the original action continues if its actor is still capable; otherwise it stops. Damage alone does not automatically cancel the action. Forced movement never provokes.

Leaving melee reach voluntarily, casting a spell beside an enemy, standing, stowing and retrieving items are the intended triggers established in discussion. Drawing as part of an attack stays part of that attack. Timing: commit the action when declared; check targets and capability again after interruption; pay an additional printed HP/item cost only when continuing into its resolution. If interrupted permanently, the committed action is spent but an unspent potion or HP cost is not consumed.

Player-controlled creatures — agreed

Creature cards must print attack and defense attributes. The controlling player rolls those printed creature attributes, not their character’s attribute. When an NPC attacks a player-controlled summon, its controller rolls the summon’s defense. When the summon attacks, its controller makes the attack roll. Use the ordinary single-roll attack/defense outcome mapping. A player-controlled attacker does not also cause a second player defense roll.

A summon disappears when its controller becomes unconscious or dies. An uncommanded summon does nothing; existing effects and conditions still resolve.

NPC-only resolution — approved October 16, 2026

Either a player or the DA assuming the player role can roll for NPC-only actions. For an NPC attacking another NPC, roll the defending NPC’s printed attribute named by the attack, with the applicable modifiers. Read the attacking creature’s Weak / Standard / Strong defense outcomes. Make only one roll, not an opposed pair.

For consequential NPC healing or another task, the same choice of roller uses the acting NPC’s printed attribute and outcomes. This does not transfer control of the NPC to the person handling the dice. Existing player-character and player-controlled creature procedures remain unchanged.

For example, when a bandit attacks an allied guard with an Agility-defense attack, a player or the DA rolls the guard’s Agility defense and reads the bandit’s card. Off-screen events may be resolved by DA judgment without rolling through unseen combat.

Stability and ordinary movement

Stability — approved: all characters and creatures start at 0; only an explicit trait, ability or item raises it, maximum 3, highest source only. It consumes forced movement once for the initial target and once for each new creature struck in a collision chain. Stop when movement is exhausted; never charge a creature twice. It does not resist Prone, grapples or conditions. See @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.3292b6a49dcf7236]{Stability} for a worked example. Collision timing approved October 16, 2026: resolve contact collision damage from movement remaining on arrival, then deduct the new member’s Stability before further travel. Applicable resistance still reduces damage.

Agreed: falling deals 3 HP per 2 squares fallen. Rounding and damage: use 3 × floor(distance / 2), physical damage with ordinary physical resistance; falls under 2 squares deal no automatic damage. Exceptional landing surfaces and circumstances are DA rulings.

Agreed: climbing and swimming use difficult-terrain movement cost, normally 2 per square, unless an ability changes it. Impossible surfaces and impassable currents do not become traversable merely by spending movement. Roll only when uncertainty has consequences. Cards can improve the ordinary activity.

Jumping — approved: broad jump up to max(1, 2 + Agility) squares; high jump up to max(0, 1 + floor(Agility / 2)) squares. Each square traveled spends movement; a broad jump needs 2 squares of approach, otherwise halve its maximum, rounded down (minimum 1). A high jump needs no approach. Land in a legal supported free square; no extra movement or passage through barriers. Negative Agility can mean no full square of high-jump clearance, not inability to hop over a small obstacle. Obstacles below a square and risky landings are adjudicated normally. No roll for a clear, safe jump within these limits; risky execution can call for Agility. These values are approved; specialist movement cards retain their explicit exceptions.

Consequence vocabulary

A consequence is what is at stake: harm, lost time, exposure, lost supplies, a worsened position or an opportunity that closes. A complication introduces an additional problem while retaining whatever progress the roll achieved. A benefit adds a useful advantage. State the stakes before rolling. Weak is progress, not automatic success; Strong is success with the printed result. Natural 111 adds a complication to Weak; 666 adds a benefit to Strong.

Use 1 Bane for a meaningful obstacle, 2 for a severe obstacle, 3 for an exceptional obstacle that remains possible. Use Boons symmetrically for real help or advantageous circumstances. These are DA guidance bands, not target numbers. Cancel Boons/Banes and apply the existing net cap of 3. Do not roll impossible attempts or apply the same obstacle twice under different names. Group progress and binary/cumulative task targets keep their existing rules.

Magic boundaries — agreed

Countermagic uses defensive interference and disruption; a separate generic spell cancellation system is not required. Healing used against a healing-harmed unwilling creature resolves as an attack spell, like Flame Dart: use the spell’s printed attribute and result as Life damage, normal attack targeting and resistance. Keep the healing spell’s action, range, free hand and upfront life cost. Beneficial recovery riders do not help that target. Eligible creature cards must print the appropriate defense attribute; no extra opposed save is added. Ordinary willing healing retains its existing procedure.

Approved by Bruce, October 13, 2026. Every character and creature starts with Stability 0. An ancestry trait, ability, equipment card or printed creature trait must explicitly grant a higher value. Stability is not calculated from attributes, ancestry size, armor, HP or level. Use the highest applicable grant, never their sum, to a maximum of 3.

Stability consumes the movement of a push, pull or throw, minimum 0. Apply the initial target’s Stability once before it moves. When the moving group strikes a new creature, that creature’s Stability consumes remaining movement once as it joins the chain, after contact collision damage resolves. If none remains, the group stops. Never charge the same creature twice during one forced movement, even if several occupied squares collide.

Stability does not resist Prone, grappling, conditions or damage. It does not reduce voluntary movement or a thrown projectile’s range. A printed push of 1 can therefore move a Stability-0 target but not a Stability-1 target; its other effects still resolve. A stopped push does not erase the attack’s damage or conditions.

Example: a push of 5 strikes a creature with Stability 1, leaving 4. It moves one normal square, leaving 3, then strikes a creature with Stability 2. That new contact deals 3 collision damage to both participants, subject to applicable resistance. The newly struck creature’s Stability then consumes 2, leaving 1 for the moving group: enough to move one more normal square before stopping.

Use the existing terrain and collision rules. Spending Stability does not itself create damage. Collision timing — approved October 16, 2026: resolve contact collision damage using the movement remaining on arrival, then deduct the new member’s Stability before further travel. This preserves an impact even when the new member stops the chain. Stability resists displacement; applicable resistance reduces damage.

Crowded moving groups — approved October 16, 2026

Move the creatures together along the forced-movement path. They must finish in separate legal spaces. If the group cannot fit, stop at the last position where everyone can fit. The DA determines the exact arrangement.

Placement cannot send a creature through a wall or grant extra forward movement. The original mover’s one-square backward bounce still applies where possible. Use the existing collision damage and Stability rules; placement does not erase an impact. No separate formation or packing procedure is required.

7 · Beyond the Battlefield

Heroes of Legend · Player’s Book

The road matters. So do the people at its end. A warm welcome, a sound bridge and a name remembered at the right moment can carry your company farther than another weapon. Your abilities include ways to navigate these scenes, but you always begin with what your hero says and does.

Explore with purpose

Tell the DA what you examine, how you approach, and what you hope to learn. If lifting the rug reveals the trapdoor, you find it by lifting the rug. No perception roll is needed to discover a fact your action plainly reveals.

When searching involves uncertainty and a meaningful consequence, the DA calls for Reason. When someone might perceive your concealed hero, roll Agility to remain Hidden; the observer does not make an opposed roll. You need a plausible place to hide. Dice do not make you disappear in open view.

Active searching or attempting to hide in combat costs a Main Action unless an ability says otherwise. Hidden is universal, not separately tracked for each observer. Attacking or openly revealing yourself ends it. The DA judges whether movement maintains actual concealment. Invisible is different: you cannot be seen, but your location is not necessarily unknown.

Before an unscripted roll, establish what progress means and what the consequences are. A Weak search might narrow the location without exposing the answer; a Weak concealment attempt might reach cover while leaving evidence of where you went. These examples are possibilities, not automatic effects that override the scene.

Consequences that matter

A consequence is what is at stake: injury, lost time, exposure, spent supplies, a worse position or a closing opportunity. A complication adds a problem while preserving any progress already earned. A benefit gives a useful advantage. The DA explains the stakes before asking for the roll.

If you can repeat an attempt indefinitely without cost, danger or changed circumstances, the table may be better served by describing the time and completing it. If failure would seal an escape route or alert a guard, say so before rolling. Weak always means its stated progress, not an unannounced success or an automatic failure.

Work as a group

Group checks occur outside combat. The DA sets a progress target and states whether the task is binary or cumulative. Each participating character rolls an appropriate attribute, contributing 1 progress on Weak, 2 on Standard, or 3 on Strong. Add the contributions and compare the total to the target.

For a binary task, meet the target in that attempt or the task is not completed. For a cumulative task, retain progress between attempts as the task allows. The DA states the time and consequence of each attempt. You can provide Aid or contribute your own group roll, not both to the same attempt.

> Example — the swollen gate. Three heroes heave against a gate before a patrol > arrives. The DA sets a binary target of 7. Weak, Strong and Strong contribute > 1 + 3 + 3 = 7: the gate opens. Weak, Standard and Strong would total 6; the gate > would stay shut and the declared consequence would follow. Pushing a boulder > uphill might instead retain those 6 progress for a later attempt.

Crafting, deriving recipes and wound treatment do not use group checks. Their individual procedures and daily limits remain in force.

Travel and the outdoors

Ordinary travel does not require routine rolls, and HOL has no exhaustion track. The DA calls for a roll when weather, pursuit, a dangerous route or another specific circumstance creates a consequence. Supplies and time still matter. Decide what your company carries, shares, buys or obtains with its abilities.

Foraging expertise comes from an appropriate environment card. It is not a universal permission to identify every edible mushroom. Other heroes can still inspect the land, collect something they already recognize, or help in a way the scene permits. Specialist cards provide their own outcomes and limitations.

Climbing and swimming normally cost 2 movement per square, like difficult terrain. This does not make a sheer unsupported wall climbable or an impassable current safe. A specialist ability can improve the activity. Roll only when the execution is uncertain and the consequence matters.

Jumping and falling

A running broad jump reaches max(1, 2 + Agility) squares. It needs two squares of approach; without that approach, halve the maximum, rounding down to a minimum of 1. A high jump reaches max(0, 1 + floor(Agility ÷ 2)) squares and needs no approach. Spend movement for the distance traveled and land in a legal, supported, free square.

Zero high-jump squares does not mean you cannot hop over a low obstacle. The grid measures large clearances. Safe jumps within your limits need no roll; a risky landing can call for Agility. Jumping does not grant extra movement or passage through a barrier.

Falling deals 3 physical damage per complete 2 squares fallen. Round the distance down to complete pairs before multiplying; normal physical resistance applies. A fall of 5 squares deals 6 damage before resistance. A fall under 2 squares has no automatic falling damage. Exceptional surfaces and landing circumstances are DA rulings.

Talk, bargain and persuade

Speak for your character, summarize what they say, or use a mixture of both. Explain what you want and why the other person might agree. The DA portrays their interests, knowledge and limits. A roll resolves uncertainty; it does not erase their motives.

Use the attribute printed on a social ability. Without one, the DA calls for an attribute appropriate to the approach. Guile might carry a deceptive bargain; Knowledge might establish a technical argument; Reason might find the important contradiction. A useful fact or appropriate gesture can make a roll unnecessary.

A scar's intimidation Boon or persuasion Bane applies when the scar actually influences the interaction. The DA decides that circumstance, just as they decide whether a wound affects a physical activity. Personality and allegiance remain choices, not penalties assigned by a condition table.

Magic in your hands

Magic is learned through abilities and disciplines. There are no spell slots or mana pools. A spell uses the same action, attribute and outcome structure as another ability, with its printed requirements and costs. An attack spell still produces its Weak result on a Weak roll; it does not simply fizzle.

You choose a card before rolling. A line, rectangle or placed area must use its printed dimensions and range. Connected placed squares share edges. Decide targets and any damage-type choice before rolling. An illustration or evocative description does not silently make the area larger or add a condition.

Defensive interference and disruption are supplied by abilities. There is no universal spell-cancellation roll. Casting beside an enemy can provoke an opportunity attack; resolve it before continuing the spell if still capable.

Beast forms keep your own HP, attributes and wounds. They are not replaceable HP pools. Use the form's printed actions and equipment restrictions. A form does not import an entire monster entry or grant spellcasting if its rules forbid it.

Moser's law of conservation of Life energy

Healing magic transfers life energy; it does not create it freely. A Novice healing spell costs its caster 1 HP, an Adept spell 3 HP, and a Master spell 7 HP. Pay the full cost before rolling. This cost bypasses all resistance and must leave the caster above 0 HP. You cannot begin a healing spell by sacrificing your last HP. The cost applies regardless of the tradition used to describe the spell.

Healing requires a free hand. Restore the outcome's printed fixed HP, reduce it by the recipient's Life resistance, and restore at least 1 if HP is missing. Never exceed maximum HP. Healing does not erase wounds or reverse Last Words. Potions have their own fixed value and inventory procedure, without a spell outcome roll or caster cost.

> Example — energy has a price. A Novice healer at 5 HP pays 1 and falls to 4, > then rolls the spell. If its outcome restores 4 HP to a companion with Life > resistance 2, the companion regains 2. The caster cannot use the same spell at > 1 HP, because paying first would leave them at 0.

A healing spell can attack a creature whose profile says healing harms it. Use the spell's attack attribute, range and cost. Its HP result becomes Life damage; beneficial recovery riders do not help that target. This follows the ordinary player-roll procedure, with no extra opposed save.

Make, identify and derive

A crafting card grants the capability to work; a recipe describes the specific thing you can make. Recipes specify permission, tools, materials, time and output. Choose the recipes granted when learning your crafting ability. Ordinary Recipe Study offers additional eligible recipes through DP. Other recipes can be found or derived; they are not automatically on sale for coins.

Acquire the actual ingredients. Foraged materials need not be carried indefinitely; carried bundles use their printed Bulk and inventory die. Complete the recipe's full time, roll the crafting card's attribute, and increase one existing product supply by 1/2/3 inventory steps as the recipe allows. Starting from out, the first step is d4. Never exceed the recipe's cap. Check carried material supply after use.

Derivation is reverse engineering, not the same as identification. Identification cards reveal what their outcomes say; an item may require that understanding before use. A magical sword may work at once, while a tome may remain unusable until understood. A derivation card specifies its target and work interval. Exceptional objects can require years of accumulated work. No group crafting or group derivation shortens it.

Rest and development

The DA determines whether a place is safe enough to spend saved DP. Level awards are milestones, not payment for each defeated creature. Keep a record of purchases, prerequisites, recipes and scars so your development remains clear.

A wound may require repeated daily treatment even after you are ready to adventure. An inn, a friendly workshop, a healer's garden or a camp among allies can become part of the story. Rest restores what its rule says it restores. It does not refund Grit, remove a permanent scar, or refill a bottle whose inventory die is out.

A familiar greeting can open a door that gold cannot. An inscription can preserve an enemy's warning long after the enemy is dust. Languages tell you whom your hero can understand and which voices shaped their life. They do not determine ancestry, allegiance or character.

Choose your languages

Begin with Common and one other ordinary language learned in the community that raised you. Common is the campaign's shared trade language; the DA may give it a local name. Choose your other language with the DA from the list below or the campaign's equivalent. Any ancestry may know any language. Culture suggests where you learned it, rather than imposing a compulsory choice.

Record the language's actual name, not just “regional” or “community language.” If Common was your only home language, choose another ordinary language learned through neighbors, work or travel. This starting choice is separate from your culture's discipline and ability pair and costs no DP.

Apply explicit extra grants afterward. A Foot in Two Worlds grants two additional ordinary spoken languages. Choose two distinct languages you do not already know; it does not grant another culture's abilities. A signed language is an ordinary language when the campaign uses it, but a grant restricted to spoken languages does not include it.

Unless a grant says otherwise, knowing a language includes speaking, understanding, and reading and writing its usual script, if it has one. A grant that specifically says spoken, understands or cannot speak keeps that restriction. Record such limits beside the language. Speaking a language does not require a separate skill rating, and attributes grant no automatic extra languages.

Ordinary languages

These are starting options, not a required history of the world. Their names describe familiar traditions; anyone raised among their speakers may learn them. Each row is one language unless it explicitly asks you to name a particular one.

LanguageWhere you might learn or encounter it

DwarvenDeep halls, quarry towns and craft communities; records of lineage, work and agreements.

Uncommon and ancient languages

These languages are not included in an unrestricted ordinary language grant. Choose one only when a grant explicitly allows it or the DA makes it an ordinary option for the campaign before character creation. Their availability reflects the setting, not a higher numerical bonus.

DraconicSpeaking with dragons and their learned allies; reading draconic inscriptions. Kobold is a separate language.
